lesson.title: Karn's Fix for a Timer That Couldn't Tell Which ACK Was Which
lesson.summary: Karn's algorithm prevents TCP from corrupting its RTT and retransmission timeout estimates by refusing to use timing samples from any segment that had to be retransmitted, since there is no way to know which transmission an ACK actually confirms.
lesson.body:
The RTO calculation from the previous chapter depends entirely on accurate RTT samples: measure the time from sending a segment to receiving its ACK, and feed that measurement into the SRTT and RTTVAR formulas. This works cleanly as long as each segment is sent exactly once. But when a segment is retransmitted, and an ACK finally arrives, the sender faces a genuine ambiguity that has no way to be resolved from the ACK alone: does this ACK acknowledge the original transmission, which was simply delayed and is only now arriving along with confirmation, or does it acknowledge the retransmission, meaning the original really was lost? A TCP sender receiving that ACK cannot tell which of the two transmissions it is responding to, because the ACK does not carry a timestamp indicating which copy of the segment prompted it (at least not without additional mechanisms beyond plain sequence numbers).

This is exactly the ambiguity problem Phil Karn identified, and it matters because either wrong guess corrupts the RTT estimate in a dangerous way. If the sender assumes the ACK confirms the original transmission but it actually confirms the retransmission, the measured "RTT" will be far too short, since the clock should have started at the retransmission, not the original send. A too-short RTT sample drags SRTT down and shrinks the RTO, making the timer fire too eagerly on the very next occasion, which risks a spiral of unnecessary retransmissions. If instead the sender assumes the ACK confirms the retransmission but it actually confirms the original, the measured RTT will be far too long, inflating SRTT and the RTO unnecessarily. Either mistake feeds bad data into an estimator that the entire connection's loss-detection timing depends on.

Karn's algorithm resolves this not by trying to guess correctly, but by refusing to guess at all: any segment that has been retransmitted is simply excluded from RTT sampling entirely. Its ACK, whenever it arrives, is used to advance the sender's understanding of what data has been received, but it is never fed into the SRTT and RTTVAR calculations. Only segments that were sent exactly once and whose ACK arrived without any retransmission in between are trusted as timing samples. This keeps the RTO estimator free of the systematic bias that ambiguous samples would otherwise introduce, at the cost of occasionally having fewer samples available during periods of loss, which is judged an acceptable tradeoff given how badly a corrupted estimate could behave.

Karn's algorithm is typically paired with a second rule concerning the backoff behavior described in the retransmission timer chapter. When a timeout occurs and a segment is retransmitted, the RTO is doubled through exponential backoff. Karn's rule says that this backed-off RTO value should be retained and reused for any further retransmissions of that same segment, rather than immediately recalculating a fresh RTO from SRTT and RTTVAR, and the estimator should not resume normal sampling until an ACK is received for a segment that did not need to be retransmitted at all. Together, these two pieces, excluding retransmitted segments from RTT samples, and holding the backed-off timer value until a clean sample reappears, prevent a period of loss or congestion from feeding misleading data back into the very timer that is supposed to detect loss and congestion in the first place.
